newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN MINISTER WARNS TIME SCARCE IN LABOUR ROW.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN MINISTER WARNS TIME SCARCE IN LABOUR ROW.

text.p: South African labour minister Tito Mboweni on Friday urged parties to revise their positions on controversial proposed new labour laws or risk not having the legislation passed in parliament this year.
"Time is now of the essence. The round of consultations is coming to a close and the willingness of the parties to move with speed is critical for collective success," he told a news briefing.
The Basic Conditions of Employment Bill is due to be tabled in parliament by September 15 and has to be ready to be signed by Cabinet on August 18.
It will be sent for printing on September 3 and parliament goes into recess on November 14.

The bill has sparked a series of clashes between business and labour with the 1.9 million Congress of South African Trade Unions staging a national strike on the issue on June 2 and threatening more action in August.
Addressing reporters after meeting the country's second largest union federation, the Federation of Unions of South Africa (FEDUSA), to discuss the bill, Mboweni said:
"Failure to reach a solution may lead to the bill being withdrawn."
He said it was likely the ANC would be the only party to support the bill in parliament.
"It is therefore critical that there is agreement from the social partners," he said.
FEDUSA president Mary Malete said: "We urge the bill to go through parliament. It should set up minimum standards (of employment) as opposed to the best standards possible."
Mboweni on Thursday held a follow-up meeting with Cosatu after a first round of bilateral talks last week.
"It was difficult. It's quite clear we still have to find each other," he commented.
Little progress had been made on the controversial issue of reducing working hours and variation of certain provisions of the bill in individual cases.

Cosatu is pushing for a 40-hour working week to be phased in over not more than five years, six months' maternity leave of which at least four are paid, double pay for Sunday work and no downward variation of basic conditions of employment.
Business is worried about provisions which could raise employment costs to the point of creating obstacles to new jobs.
Mboweni said, however, government had proposed a schedule in the bill which indicated that the goal of a 40-hour working week should be a common goal.
"The task will be to bring business to accept the schedule. No harm will be done in including in schedule a commitmnet to 40 hours," he said.
Government and Cosatu decided to set up a technical team to tackle "thorny issues over the next week," Mboweni said, enabling him to report back to the ANC's national working committee on July 28.
Further follow-up meetings are also scheduled with business and FEDUSA next week.

Mboweni said the possibility of tripartite talks with government, labour and business were "zero" at the moment and government would continue focusing on bilateral discussions in an effort to reach consensus.
-- Vera von Lieres, Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
